posts.note: Satirical sales-pitch post ('This is a joke'); present-tense claims about 5-day remission treatment only, no forward-looking statements.
Reaction to the CDC provisional 2022 suicide report. Author says he 'did see coming' the record numbers (retrospective, not logged).
Satire of gift-card text scams; no sincere forward-looking claims.
Essay against 'passion' as a credential in the mental health space; no forecasts.
Defamation law explainer, part III of a series; advice only, no forecasts.
Satire about newsletter income. Satirical advice to readers ('Your audience will reward you with 10s of dollars a month') has no sincere predictive reading; not logged.
Monarch eTNS (Neurosigma) as an answer to the stimulant shortage. Author prescribes it at Fermata and Acacia. Footnote 5 announces his own TMS-for-ADHD paper.
Generative AI essay written from vacation; one borderline general claim about the ceiling of generative AI logged.
Fire as product-market-fit essay. Metaphorical claims about fire ('It will do so again') not logged; one reported third-party AI warning logged with own_claim false.
2020 podcast transcript on policing and race, republished 2023; two borderline generalizations by the author logged. Third-party speakers (Master Sergeant, Sequoiah, Osei) not logged.

statements.quote: It’s not going to get better until we call a spade a spade.
statements.context: Post on the CDC provisional report of 49,449 US suicide deaths in 2022, a 2.6% rise and a record. After listing failures of current mental health treatment (inaccurate diagnoses, ineffective treatments, refusal to pay for effective ones, 988 calls redirected out of state), the author asserts the crisis and the suicide numbers will not improve until the field admits the failure.
statements.horizon_text: until we call a spade a spade
statements.note: Negative call on the mental health/suicide trend; the condition is rhetorical. Earlier line claims he 'did see coming' the record numbers (retrospective).

statements.quote: If physicians prescribe this medical device, which is not a controlled substance, they may avoid stimulants in many cases.
statements.context: Post on the Neurosigma Monarch eTNS device (FDA de novo cleared for ADHD ages 7-12, prescribed off-label for adults) as an answer to the stimulant shortage. The author, whose practice Fermata prescribes it, says that if physicians prescribe the device they may avoid stimulants in many cases.
statements.note: Hedged conditional about prescribing practice. Author discloses no financial tie to Neurosigma but prescribes the device at Fermata and Acacia Mental Health.

statements.quote: Every stimulant prescription—these days—means there will be a subsequent game of “find the pharmacy” to fill the script
statements.context: Same Monarch eTNS post. The author describes the ongoing stimulant shortage: every stimulant prescription these days leads to a hunt for a pharmacy with stock, and pharmacies cannot legally say what is in stock because of an opioid settlement.
statements.note: Borderline: habitual present about the ongoing stimulant shortage; implies the shortage persists for prescriptions written now.

statements.quote: This is how we solve the ADHD treatment crisis—with better treatments!
statements.context: Same Monarch eTNS post. After pricing Monarch at about $1000 plus about $45 per 7 days of pads (insurance may cover kids 7-12; adults pay out of pocket) versus roughly $400/month list for Mydayis, the author states the ADHD treatment crisis gets solved with better treatments (non-invasive devices) rather than with stimulants.
statements.note: Thesis statement that reads as a claim about how the crisis will be resolved. Earlier line: 'the only real answer I can see is getting more effective treatments to more people'.

statements.quote: I don't think we solve ADHD at scale by doing things that aren't scalable.
statements.context: Same Monarch eTNS post. The author doubts ADHD care gets solved at scale through non-scalable approaches (stimulants constrained by DEA quotas and supply chains) and argues for scalable device treatment instead.
statements.note: Hedged negative call about the path to solving ADHD care at scale.

statements.quote: At this point, there's a hard limit on stimulant medications, and there's a hard limit on the amount of frustration anybody is going to put up with to prescribe them.
statements.context: Same Monarch eTNS post. The author says stimulant supply has a hard limit and prescriber frustration with the shortage also has a hard limit, implying prescribers will stop tolerating the hassle of stimulant prescribing and move to alternatives.
statements.note: Implicit forecast that prescriber tolerance of stimulant hassle runs out; no timing given.

statements.quote: I'm also about to publish a paper on getting ADHD into remission—in 5 days— with transcranial magnetic stimulation.
statements.context: Footnote 5 of the Monarch eTNS post. The author says he is about to publish a paper on getting ADHD into remission in 5 days with transcranial magnetic stimulation, adds that he was surprised by the result, and says he does not know how durable the effect will be.
statements.note: Own research output (CONTROL candidate). Same footnote: 'I don't know how long that effect will be durable'.

statements.quote: you will get a very brutal regression to the mean. At best, you're going to be presented with the average of what we think, with some guard rails about its awfulness.
statements.context: Post on the disappointment with generative AI, written from vacation. The author argues that a model trained on average human output, minus the human ability to tell nonsense from sense, regresses to the mean: at best generative AI presents the average of what humans think, with guard rails. He later names ChatGPT and Stable Diffusion and compares poorly designed generative AI to mendacious politicians.
statements.note: Borderline: general claim about the ceiling of generative AI rather than a dated call.

statements.quote: AI marketers figured that out, and they warned us about how dangerous it was. They warned us it could end the world.
statements.context: Essay using fire as the model of undeniable product-market fit (dangerous, disruptive, never abandoned). The author says AI marketers used the same fire-like pitch and warned that AI could end the world; he cites it as an example of fire-standard marketing, not as his own expectation.
statements.note: Third-party warning reported, not adopted (own_claim false). Logged for recall only.

statements.quote: For a long time, Black America has known to watch out when you talk to the cops because they can kill you. Nothing's going to stop them if they want to.
statements.context: Podcast transcript recorded in 2020 about race and policing after George Floyd's death, republished 2023. The author, as narrator, says Black Americans know police can kill them and nothing is going to stop the police if they want to; he calls the 'bad apples' explanation insufficient and says police killings of Black people have never been ruled unlawful.
statements.note: 2020 recording republished 2023. Footnote 2 adds that since the recording a few officers were found guilty, but 'the standard, however, remains the same'.

statements.quote: You're going to pull that trigger. More often than not. And that's about a thousand times a year.
statements.context: Same 2020 policing transcript. The author argues that police called to mental health crises, armed and told to protect themselves with no consequence for shooting, will pull the trigger more often than not, about a thousand times a year, and that Black mentally ill people are more likely to be killed.
statements.note: Borderline: hypothetical second-person generalization about police behavior; the yearly figure is a present rate, not a target.

statements.quote: If we use the standard P value from science for the evaluation of health plans, we will solve a lot of arguments!
statements.context: Advocacy piece proposing that mental health parity be enforced with statistical tests: compare spending across every ICD-10 diagnosis for general medical versus mental health/substance use care with a two-sample t-test and Bonferroni correction at the p<0.05 standard. The author claims applying the scientific null-hypothesis standard to health plans will resolve many parity disputes. Addressed to the Department of Labor and 'Big Health'.
statements.note: Conditional on adoption of the proposal; no timing. Later lines about plans failing the test are normative ('it's on them to prove').
